title: Ontario Superior Court dismisses lawsuit against Popeyes
html:
A lawsuit accusing Popeyes Louisiana Kitchen PLKI-Q of selling “unsafe” chicken in Ontario restaurants has been struck down, after an Ontario Superior Court judge ruled that allegations of food safety breaches were not relevant to the civil dispute over the alleged breach of contract between the fast-food giant and the supplier.

The lawsuit was filed in May 2025 by Toronto-based ADP Direct Poultry Ltd., a former chicken supplier to Popeyes. It made a number of claims against the company, some franchisees and others, including for breach of contract, negligence, and unlawful interference with economic relations. It also included accusations that Popeyes franchisees bought chicken from an unauthorized seller that in some cases sold “rotten” meat to Toronto-area restaurants.

But those food safety allegations amounted to “a diversion from a deficient contract claim for ADP’s loss of the Popeyes business after 2024,” Justice R. Lee Akazaki wrote in the decision, filed in court on Thursday.

If true, the presence of unsafe ingredients in a food supply chain could form the basis for a legal claim or a class action for food poisoning, brought on behalf of restaurant customers or affected franchisees, the judge wrote. But if the allegations are true, “there is no discernable duty of care owed to ADP or mechanism of harm to ADP,” Justice Akazaki wrote.

The judge gave ADP 30 days to prepare a new amended statement of claim against Popeyes and its parent company.

In addition to the fast-food company, ADP’s lawsuit named a number of Popeyes franchisees, a man who was the alleged supplier of unsafe meat, and a company that manages Restaurant Brands’ QSR-T supply chain. A former Popeyes executive was also later added to the lawsuit.

The statement of claim alleged that at least two dozen Popeyes locations in the Greater Toronto Area made purchases from the unauthorized supplier, who sometimes stored the raw chicken in a residential garage, and transported it to restaurants in vehicles that lacked proper refrigeration or freezing procedures.

ADP began supplying fresh and frozen packaged chicken to Restaurant Brands in late 2021. But beginning the following year, the company began receiving an unusual number of complaints from franchisees about spoiled meat, which the ADP said were illegitimate. It was unclear why it would have received complaints about meat that did not come from the ADP facility.

Then, the supplier received a tip about the unauthorized meat sales, which it decided to investigate – first, in surveillance conducted by the president of ADP, and later, over months, by private investigators the company hired.

ADP reported its findings to Restaurant Brands in 2022 and 2024, and executives told the supplier they would look into it. Restaurant Brands said that they found no evidence of the allegations. At the end of 2024, it cut off ADP’s supply contract, according to ADP.

When the lawsuit was filed, Restaurant Brands said the poultry processor was “lashing out after losing our business for a variety of legitimate reasons.” ADP in response added a defamation claim to its lawsuit, which the judge also struck out in Thursday’s decision.

Justice Akazaki wrote that ADP had failed to prove a civil conspiracy, where the defendants falsely reported the company as the source of the unsafe meat.

“The conspiracy pleadings regarding the introduction of unsafe meat into the restaurant supply chain are not inherently implausible,” he wrote. “However, ADP’s attempts to insert itself as the victim of the unsafe meat conspiracy appears to require more artifice than the described facts can bear.”

The judge also raised concerns about ADP’s claim of a breach of contract. ADP claimed it lost investments it had made related to an understanding of future business with Restaurant Brands, as well as opportunities with other customers.

But the supplier’s official contract with Restaurant Brands had expired in February 2023, and the orders ADP received from Popeyes in 2024 did not constitute a new binding contract, the judge wrote. The chain “was free to stop doing business with ADP.”

ADP’s filing had also accused Popeyes of violations of Canada’s Competition Act, alleging the chain had made false representations to the public about the safety of its restaurant meals. But that statute is “regulatory and quasi-criminal,” Justice Akazaki wrote, adding Popeyes would be answerable to the public and not to a private litigant for such a violation.

In his conclusions, the judge struck out the statement of claim in its entirety for “failing to disclose a cause of action.” He also struck out any claims against the rest of the defendants, with costs.

Justice Akazaki wrote that ADP’s claims of a breach of contract and misrepresentation could be salvaged if the company can show facts of a supply agreement that was in place after February 2023; bad faith in the breach of the agreement; and fraud or deceit by Popeyes.

If the new statement of claim is not made, the Popeyes defendants could bring a motion for dismissal of the case, with costs.
summary: Accusations that franchisees bought unsafe chicken from unauthorized seller was a diversion from contract claim, judge rules
